nameStory: Clustered mountainmint gets its name from its flowers, which bunch together in tight, rounded clusters at the top of the stem, looking like little white pom-poms. The "mountainmint" part comes from its membership in the mint family and its refreshing, minty fragrance - though it doesn't necessarily grow on mountains! Early botanists grouped these aromatic native plants together as "mountain mints" to distinguish them from the true mints that often grow in wetter areas.
description: Clustered mountainmint is a native perennial herb that stands 1-3 feet tall with a bushy, upright growth habit. It produces distinctive white flower clusters that sit like fluffy caps on top of square stems, surrounded by pale, silvery-white leaves called bracts. The plant has a pleasant minty smell when crushed and belongs to the same family as basil, oregano, and other culinary herbs. It's a pollinator magnet, especially beloved by butterflies and native bees.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded clusters of tiny white flowers perched at stem tips, surrounded by distinctive pale, whitish-green bracts that look almost silvery. The flower heads resemble small white pincushions and have a sweet, minty fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are lance-shaped and toothless along the edges, with a smooth texture. When crushed, they release a strong, pleasant minty aroma that's immediately recognizable.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple square stems typical of the mint family. The stems feel distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers.

idTips.label: Bracts
idTips.description: The pale, whitish-green leaves directly beneath each flower cluster are the key feature - they're much lighter in color than the regular leaves and give the whole flower head a frosted appearance.

habitat: Look for clustered mountainmint in partially shaded woodlands with dappled sunlight, woodland edges, and moist meadows throughout New England. It prefers well-drained but consistently moist soils and often grows alongside other native wildflowers like wild bergamot and goldenrod. You'll find it in areas that get some sun but aren't completely exposed.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as square stems with opposite leaves. The distinctive minty fragrance is already present if you crush a leaf.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with showy white flower clusters surrounded by pale bracts. This is when the plant is most attractive to butterflies and easiest to spot.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads, and stems may persist. The minty smell becomes less pronounced as leaves begin to dry.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and seed heads. Look for dead square stems as evidence of last year's growth.

funFact: Native Americans used mountainmints as natural insect repellent, crushing the leaves and rubbing them on their skin - the same compounds that give it that refreshing mint smell also keep mosquitoes and other bugs away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other mountainmints in the same genus, but clustered mountainmint has the most densely packed, rounded flower heads. Memory trick: "Clustered" means the flowers are really bunched together, unlike the more spread-out flower arrangements of its cousins like narrowleaf or Virginia mountainmint.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - these "mints" aren't closely related to the spearmint or peppermint you might grow in your garden, though they're in the same large plant family. Mountainmints are uniquely North American natives that evolved here, while culinary mints mostly came from Europe and Asia.
compareHints: Clustered mountainmint has the most compact, densely rounded flower heads of all the mountainmints - they look like tight white buttons. Narrowleaf mountainmint has much thinner leaves and looser flower clusters, while Virginia mountainmint has broader leaves with visible teeth along the edges. The pale bracts surrounding clustered mountainmint's flowers are also more prominent and silvery than those of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Narrowleaf mountainmint stands out from its mountain mint relatives by having the thinnest leaves in the group—often less than 1/4 inch wide compared to the broader leaves of clustered mountainmint or Virginia mountain mint.

Among New England's mountain mints, Virginia mountain mint stands out with its very narrow, lance-shaped leaves - much thinner than the broad leaves of clustered mountain mint or the fuzzy, whitish leaves of hoary mountain mint.
Among the mountainmints, hoary mountainmint is easily distinguished by its uniquely fuzzy, silvery appearance - the other species have green, relatively smooth leaves.
Unlike its mountain mint relatives that have opposite paired leaves, Whorled Mountain Mint's leaves circle the stem in distinctive whorls.
Torrey's mountainmint differs from its more common relatives like Virginia mountain mint by its narrower leaves and denser flower clusters.
